transcript:
"This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour."
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herst.
President Trump is continuing campaign stops with Republican candidates this week ahead
of the upcoming midterm elections.
NPR's Shonda Lee-Stuster has more.
President Trump is hitting the campaign trail again this week in hopes of giving Republican
candidates a boost ahead of the midterm elections.
Last month, he promised to visit 35 battleground districts to help Republican candidates.
And while he has said he would focus on swing districts, the majority of places where he
is campaigning are in Republican-heavy areas.
He is also visiting places where he made big wins during the 2024 presidential election.
One of his stops include North Carolina, where he will rally for Senate candidate Michael
Watley.
But Republicans have pulled back funding for ads for Watley across the state.
A sign of concern is Watley trails in the polls behind Democrat and former Governor
Roy Cooper.
Shonda Lee-Stuster, NPR News.
And Democrats are pushing hard to gain control of the U.S. Senate, and those efforts include
a contentious race in Florida.
As Ailey Shanes from member station WUFT reports, Democratic hopeful Angie Nixon is on the road
campaigning with Sen. Bernie Sanders.
"Give it up for Sen. Bernie Sanders!"
Sanders joins Nixon on the University of Florida campus as part of the Fight the oligarchy
tour.
Nixon is a current state representative in Florida and says she represents the working
class.
"I didn't run for office just to keep people down.
I ran to lift them up.
I ran to fight the corruption that is making our costs rise."
Nixon also supports issues like universal health care, restrictions on AI data centers,
and campaign finance reform.
Sanders says with Nixon in the Senate, he'd want to place more taxes on the wealthy and
invest more into social security.
Nixon will challenge incumbent Republican Ashley Moody.
For NPR News, I'm Ailey Shanes in Gainesville.
In France, protests over the rising cost of living and poor school conditions turned into
chaos over the weekend as demonstrators set fire to cars and buildings, including a historic
building in Lyon.
Thousands were detained.
And Emmanuel Macron says those responsible for the violence in Paris and other cities
will face justice, drawing a line in a national TV address between those protesting peacefully
and the left-wing troublemakers he blames for the destruction that shocked many.
"Hundreds of thousands of our fellow citizens demonstrated with legitimate claims, and we
should never confuse those who demonstrated peacefully with looters and rioters.
These demonstrators are worried about the cost of living and the price of fuels, worries
that find their source in the conflict happening in the Persian Gulf.
I understand their worries."
President Macron heard there through a BBC interpreter.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
More than a dozen indigenous leaders from Brazil, Peru, Colombia and Ecuador are heading
to the United Nations Conference in Vienna this week to push for stronger international
action against criminal networks that are threatening their forests and communities
in the Amazon through illegal mining and drug trafficking.
They want to target the financial networks behind the environmental issues, and they're
pushing for a bigger role in protecting their territories along with stronger indigenous
land rights.
Hollywood just had a surprisingly strong weekend.
And as NPR's Bob Bundello reports, the emphasis is definitely on the surprise.
The number one film this weekend was the martial arts action flick Street Fighter, but it's
the number two film that's causing a stir.
"I really feel you did nothing wrong."
"I did not."
In You Can See Everything, Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, who's currently serving
a prison sentence for defrauding investors, is interrogated by absurdist comedian Nathan
Fielder.
"Does any part of you worry about me being here 24/7?"
"I don't think so."
"But what if I see something that makes you look bad?"
Produced in secret, the almost three-hour movie was on no one's radar until two months
ago.
Then a scene from it went viral, as did talk of a mid-film surprise.
And this weekend, with spoiler-reverse crowds flocking to fewer than 1,000 theaters, you
can see everything posted the second-best opening ever for a documentary.
Not surprisingly, the film will expand its run next week.
Bob Bundello, NPR News.
U.S. futures contracts are trading higher this morning, NASDAQ futures up 1 percent.
I'm Janine Herbst, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: Trump continues midterm campaign stops, including North Carolina rally for Senate candidate Michael Watley
Democrat Angie Nixon campaigns in Gainesville, Florida with Senator Bernie Sanders against Ashley Moody
Protests over cost of living and school conditions in France turn violent; Macron vows justice
Indigenous leaders from Amazon countries head to UN Vienna conference to fight criminal networks
Elizabeth Holmes documentary 'You Can See Everything' posts strong weekend opening after Street Fighter tops box office
U.S. stock futures trade higher, with NASDAQ futures up 1 percent
